doc.title: Arturo Sandoval interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 12, 2023

chapter: Career, recognition and jazz in America
title: Jazz neglected by American media and television
summary: He calls it a crime that he has seen no jazz on US television in 34 years and complains that media promote trashy music; Rowe notes universities offer jazz programs for financial reasons.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: I don’t know if you’ll be able to address this or not but do you think that playing with the head more than the soul is partly an outcome of the boom in jazz education?

I’m going to tell you something. We have another problem which is even deeper and more — it’s worse than that. I strongly believe that we have a serious problem, especially in the U.S. with the appreciation and promoting, defending, protecting the immense legacy that we got in our culture about jazz. We don’t feel like that kind of appreciation in general terms. I’m talking about the radio stations, the television, the media in general. We don’t have a little bit of support. I’m going to tell you something. I’m living in the U.S. for 34 years and I consider it a crime that I never saw one minute of jazz on television. I’ll repeat that. I consider that a crime because if you go to Scandinavia or Japan or anywhere, even in Europe, all over Europe, on Saturday night, to put an example, on Saturday night at 9 P.M. you’re going to have a good chance to watch on the main network two hours of any of those jazz festivals around the world. I never saw that in the U.S. and I repeat, that’s a crime because it’s our mission, it’s our obligation to preserve that immense legacy that jazz music means to the American culture. And I’m going to add something. I strongly believe that jazz music is the most important contribution from the U.S. to the art to the world. Some people, no, most of the people don’t get it. And that’s something unacceptable. It’s something horrible, horrible. Because I always think about what they think — Louis Armstrong and Dizzy, and all those people — they are looking from the sky and they said, “Guys, what the heck are you doing with what we left you? Are you protecting this? Are you defending that? Are you promoting? Are you proud of that? Are you?” They have that question and they ask that question to us every day. And what is the reaction of the media? They promote the trashy music. The trash. You know the worst thing. And the thing that the younger generation is getting about music is not the best one. It’s probably the worst. And in terms of the lyrics for example nowadays a lot of songs they are so full of profanity you know. They say a bunch of dirty words and the younger listen to this like that’s normal, that’s okay, that’s the today music. No. That’s not today’s music. That’s trash music. That’s something horrible that we should feel ashamed for that. And I’m still waiting, I hope someday before I die I see some reactions from the media to educate the people and let them know what jazz means and how much jazz music is appreciated all over the world. A lot more than the U.S., in the U.S.

It’s a conundrum because you have almost every university in the country now, I don’t know if it’s because it was an artistic decision but more than likely it was a financial decision that having a jazz program was something that they decided to do because they could see that there would be students who would come to their colleges. Yet as you say the respect for the music generally has not kept up with that. © Fillius Jazz Archive -7-
